target_claim: In Case 3, sub-case i != 1 and j != 2 with i = 2 and k = 1, the proof selects l from N_n \ {1,2,3,k} and asserts that sigma = (1, 2, j, l, 3) is an even permutation with sigma(1)=i, sigma(2)=j, sigma(3)=k. The exclusion set is wrong: since k = 1 in this sub-case, the constraint reduces to l not in {1,2,3}, which does not exclude l = j, and the displayed 5-cycle requires l != j to even be a well-defined cycle.
source_quote:
Since $n \ge 5$, there exists an element $l \in \N_n \setminus \set {1, 2, 3, k}$.

Then, the [[Definition:Permutation on n Letters|permutation]] $\sigma = \tuple {1, 2, j, l, 3}$ is [[Definition:Even Permutation|even]] and has the desired property.
